title: Liberty Leading the People (Le 28 juillet 1830. La Liberté guidant le peuple)

museum.name: Department of Paintings of the Louvre (RF 129)

source.label: Wikipedia: commemorating the July Revolution of 1830; painted in the autumn of 1830
Wikipedia: commemorating the July Revolution of 1830

highlight.text: Delacroix depicted Liberty as both an allegorical goddess-figure and a robust woman of the people. The mound of corpses and wreckage acts as a kind of pedestal from which Liberty strides, barefoot and bare-breasted, out of the canvas and into the space of the viewer.

source.label: Wikipedia: a painting of the Romantic era

work.text: By the time Delacroix painted Liberty Leading the People, he was already the acknowledged driving force of the Romantic school in French painting.

The figure of the bourgeois of 1830, on the other hand, is magnificent. His tall hat pressed down over one ear, he holds a heavy musket convulsively grasped in his hands … This is one of Delacroix's finest creations, the truest, the most sincere, the least literary.

moment.text: That man … is the true painter who is able to extract from modern and everyday life its epic side, and to show and teach us by means of colour and drawing how great and poetical we are in our cravats and polished boots.
moment.lead: Baudelaire's call for a painter of modern life:

source.author: Charles Baudelaire
source.title: Curiosités esthétiques
source.publisher: translated in Dorothy Bussy, Eugène Delacroix (Duckworth, 1907; Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: The French government bought the painting in 1831 for 3,000 francs with the intention of displaying it in the throne room of the Palais du Luxembourg as a reminder to the "citizen-king" Louis-Philippe of the July Revolution, through which he had come to power. … the canvas hung in the palace's museum gallery for a few months before being removed due to its inflammatory political message.

matters.text: I have started work on a modern subject, a scene on the barricades … I may not have fought for my country but at least I shall have painted for her.
matters.lead: Writing to his brother that autumn:

source.author: Eugène Delacroix

matters.text: the dead body of the young man who, dressed merely in his shirt, lies with his poor naked legs stiff and uncovered is profoundly touching.
